doc.title: Karolina Strassmayer interviewed by Monk Rowe, May 25, 2023

chapter: Her music, free jazz and playing
title: Playing for herself or the audience, and presence
summary: She moved from playing to be acknowledged to giving presence and aliveness to listeners.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: That’s sort of what I was going to try to ask, when you’re sitting and composing or when you’re in the middle of an improvisation are you aware of the audience? Maybe I could say are you playing for the audience or are you playing for yourself?

Both. Maybe I can start by saying when I first started out as a musician I was definitely playing for myself. And I was playing in a way that I wanted to get respect, I wanted to get acknowledged, I wanted to be seen as somebody who can play, so really from a very sort of needy place of like yeah look I can play. But I was playing for myself and over the

years as I’ve grown as a human being I have discovered that giving with music is a great privilege. It is an experience that we can give people and what I give is actually this — what moves me, my idea of beauty, but also when I’m on stage I’m somebody who is present. I’m present for the music and for the people in that moment. And that’s really at the center. It doesn’t matter the notes, the style or this or that. It is am I here? Am I really here? Am I really present for this? And that is a gift and it’s a gift to myself because I feel really great when I can play from that place of presence and aliveness and I can be relaxed. I can trust the music. I can let the music evolve. I can really delight in what the other musicians are playing and I’ve seen the reaction of people who come to my concerts over the years. You know the biggest compliment you could give me when I was maybe 25 or 30 — “Yeah man, she can really play, the girl can really play. Do you see how she can really tear it up.” You know. That kind of — “Man she was really shredding those rhythm changes” or “she sounds like a guy when you close your eyes.” Right? This was just like oh yeah, my ego is like thank you, thank you, thank you. And now the biggest compliment or the most beautiful thing that I can get after a concert or during a concert from people is when I see that they close their eyes and they relax their face and their head just sort of moves back a little bit and to the side and they begin to connect with themselves and the music and the present moment. And when I see that then I know I’m doing it right. And that to me is really, this is what I get back when I look out into the people and there’s a certain softness in their face. There’s a certain, maybe a slight smile or there’s a wonder in their eyes where they just see like wow, they’re filled with something pleasant. A pleasant feeling. And by that I don’t mean like playing what the people like. I don’t mean that. I mean really what I like and I think people can feel from a performer whether that person is really present and is really giving. And then they don’t care. Then you can play the out shit and it touches them.
